title: Marcus Firman: Taser is 'very close to last resort'
subtitle: Aron Firman was 27 when he was killed by police, who shot him once with a Taser. His father thinks the weapon has a place, but stresses de-escalation techniques as most important.
article: Marcus Firman and his wife Christine Cowley lost their son June 24, 2010, when police shot him with a Taser in Collingwood, Ont.. Aron Firman was a physically healthy 27-year-old schizophrenic who had spent his life in and out of institutions. Police were responding to a report that he was agitated and had been hitting another person. Marcus Firman talked to us about the tragedy.

He was actually a gentle soul. Even his psychiatrist in Penetanguishene could not believe that these were the actions of Aron that were reported by police. It wouldn't have been Aron in any time that he's known him, and he's known him when Aron was angry as well.
He was diagnosed with schizophrenia when he was 21. From that point to his death he would be in and out of institutions. It is the disease. It is common for that to happen.

In my son's case, he was sitting calmly in the backyard when the police arrived. They said they approached him, they tried to lower their stance, they talked to him. A couple minutes maybe. He was only responding to some of their questions, not all. One of the witnesses said they heard the police officer say, "Well now you've earned yourself a night in jail." He's a big guy - six-foot-four. These were both big officers.
On a magical signal, they take a pace forward.

Well you have a six-foot guy approach you to grab hold of you, what are you going to do if you're sitting down? You're going to jump up pretty quick. I know I would. You're going to jump up. So he jumped up.
One officer goes round behind him. She tries to grab him from the back and he elbows her in the face.
The big (male) officer, rather than apprehending him, pushes him away to "create space." Now with the creation of space you can apply a Taser. So he pushes him away and then Tasers him, basically.
I could have told you within five minutes that there wasn't a criminal action here. So there's nothing for the SIU (Special Investigations Unit) to pursue.

Police should be accountable for their actions at all stages and again they should be held to a higher standard, not just the criminal code. Are they enforcing their policies? Are they doing what they're trained to do? Have they acted appropriately?
They have strict policies and procedures that they should be following. Were they adhered to? That is not for the SIU to judge. They only judge if there was a criminal action.

The case never saw the inside of a criminal courtroom. The chief pathologist of Ontario, Dr. Michael Pollanen, originally listed Aron's cause of death as "cardiac arrhythmia precipitated by electronic control device." The coroner's inquest into Aron's death was completed July of this year. Pollanen, who performed the autopsy, maintained that the Taser was a significant contributing factor in Aron's death, but three years later the verdict of the coroner's jury relegated the Taser to second-last on the list of contributing factors.

A jury is hearing four sides that oppose the family's position, because you have the Crown representing the coroner, you have the Crown representing the ministry, you have Taser International who supply the Crown, then you have police federation lawyers which is in support of employees of the Crown. They're going to posit a position that is in variance with that of the family, not necessarily getting to the truth. What they want to do is relieve themselves of any culpability from responsibility.
So now when a jury hears four times this, as opposed to one time of the family's view, the preponderance of the stuff being put forward to them is obviously going to skew their thinking.
Marcus said he never had a sense of justice throughout the process.

I think that's what's most depressing. I think that's quite depressing because it's the extinguishing of hope. Without hope, what do we have? You've got to have hope for a better world otherwise what's the point? We have to learn.
I understand people make mistakes. If we don't learn from those mistakes, what are we?

I believe the Taser has its use. I believe it has its use as a weapon very close to last resort. The gun is obviously the last resort, but the Taser is up there with it. It's not described as a non-lethal weapon now, it's described as a less lethal weapon, which in my understanding of the English language means it's lethal.

If he'd been appropriately trained in de-escalation, observing the signs, the outcome could have been totally different and without the use of any weapons. Really isn't that the goal? Isn't that the goal of any police force that it should end in a non-violent situation where at all possible?
